clue.text: Criminal crossing mink with a polecat

indicators.note: crossing animals breeds them together, so the letters are mixed up into a new creature

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mad scientist's illegal scheme to breed a mink with a polecat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' reads as an adjective for the breeding scheme, but it is a noun naming a kind of offender. The animals are just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with a compulsion to steal is a thief, and theft makes such a person an offender under the law.

clue.text: Joint drink party

blocks.note: the knee is a joint of the leg
to sup is to sip or drink

explanation.surface: A party where a joint and drinks are passed around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' tempts you towards cannabis, but it is the body part. A knees-up is British slang for a lively, noisy party.
explanation.definitionFit: A knees-up is an informal British term for a boisterous celebration with dancing and drinking, so it is a kind of party.

clue.text: I have brought up depression, to be clear

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing something up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: I have contracts to I've
a dent is a small hollow or depression

explanation.surface: Someone has raised their depression so that it is out in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low mood, but here it is a physical dent. 'Brought up' is the down-clue signal for turning letters around.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evident is obvious and plain to see, which is what clear means here.

clue.text: Cost of travelling coach sounds reasonable

indicators.note: a word that sounds like another is heard rather than read, so spelling may differ

blocks.note: to coach someone is to train them
fair means reasonable or just

explanation.surface: A traveller judges the price of a coach ticket to be reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a bus, but it is the verb meaning to train. Only the second half is a sound-alike: FAIR said aloud gives FARE.
explanation.definitionFit: A train fare is the price paid for a journey by rail, so it is a cost of travelling.

clue.text: Miserly old person, evidently scammed to begin with, is upset

indicators.note: what each word has to begin with is its opening letter, so only initials are kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted pensioner who has plainly been conned is distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a full story about a swindled miser, but the definition is just the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To mope is to be listless and gloomy, a way of behaving when someone feels down or unhappy.

clue.text: Fix pub providing service found on the high street

definitions.text: service found on the high street

blocks.note: to nail something is to fix it in place
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: A pub is being fixed up so that it can serve the high street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix' seems to mean repair the pub, but it is a verb for hammering in. The high street is the British term for a town's main shopping street.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon offering manicures and painted fingertips is a common shopfront business in British town centres.

clue.text: Old-fashioned inheritance excluded heir

indicators.note: what is excluded is left out, so some letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these four letters are removed

explanation.surface: An outdated will that disinherited the rightful heir.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing H, E, I and R from INHERITANCE leaves NITANCE, which must then be rearranged; the clue gives no separate signal for that rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient means very old, and something old-fashioned belongs to a much earlier time, so the two overlap loosely.

clue.text: Cloth handbag at first could be ranked most important

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening, so only the initial letter is used
letters that could be something else are possible rearrangements of themselves

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
the six letters rearranged
chief means principal or most important

explanation.surface: A fabric handbag might be rated the most important accessory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cloth handbag' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Cloth'. The anagram fodder is 'ranked', which also looks like part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A handkerchief is a small square of fabric for wiping the nose, so it is a piece of cloth.

clue.text: Country has organised crime within its borders

indicators.note: organising things puts them into a new arrangement
something within is placed inside something else

blocks.note: the outer letters of the country being clued, A at each end
the five letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A nation where the Mafia operates inside its frontiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised crime' is a stock phrase meaning the Mafia, which hides the anagram signal. 'Its borders' refers to the answer itself: the country begins and ends with A.
explanation.definitionFit: America is the everyday name for the United States, a nation and so a country.

clue.text: Will and Harry, but not quite Diana?

indicators.note: something not quite complete is missing a bit at the end

blocks.note: Diana's royal title, a female royal of Wales; its last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: The two royal brothers, set against their late mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Diana, Princess of Wales, was the mother of Prince William and Prince Harry; dropping one letter from her title gives their shared title in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: William and Harry are the sons of King Charles and both hold royal rank as male heirs of the monarch.

clue.text: Upsetting a fascist party in power is acceptable

indicators.note: upsetting something knocks it over and jumbles it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: these eight letters rearranged
the Conservatives, or Tories, were the governing British party when this was set

explanation.surface: A political claim that it is fine to annoy an extremist in government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' reads as causing offence, but it is the anagram signal. Tory is the nickname for Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Satisfactory describes something good enough to meet requirements, the same as being passable or adequate.

clue.text: Catch sight of Cinders dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and end up in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The prince spots Cinderella dancing at the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Cinders is the pet name for Cinderella, so the pantomime scene hides that the name is just seven letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To discern is to perceive or make out with the eyes, which is to notice or spot something.

clue.text: Topic of citizen in a monarchy

blocks.note: first meaning: the matter being discussed
second meaning: a person who owes allegiance to a king or queen

explanation.surface: A discussion point about the people living under a crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'of' makes it read as one phrase, but it only joins two separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the theme of a talk or essay and a person ruled over by a sovereign.

clue.text: Play back recording, including kiss for someone far from home

indicators.note: playing something back runs it the other way, so the letters are turned around
to include something is to hold it inside

blocks.note: a tape is a recording
X is the conventional sign for a kiss

explanation.surface: Replaying a recorded message with a kiss for a loved one living abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play back' sounds like replaying the message, but it signals reading the letters backwards. X for a kiss is the sign at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An expat, short for expatriate, lives outside their native country, so is a long way from where they grew up.

clue.text: Breathes in dodgy parasites

indicators.note: something dodgy is unsound or not right, so the letters are out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone accidentally inhales some nasty parasites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy' is British slang for suspect or unreliable, here just signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspirate is to draw air or matter into the lungs, so it means to inhale.

clue.text: Had group that's armed Isis held every now and then

indicators.note: something done every now and then happens at intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: a posse is a band of armed men gathered by a sheriff
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A militant group was seized and occasionally detained by Isis.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to terrorism, but Isis is just letters to pick from, and the armed group is a Wild West posse.
explanation.definitionFit: Possessed is the past tense of possess, meaning to own, which is what had means in the sense of having property.

clue.text: They write baroque poems in heartless covers

definitions.note: a pronoun and verb standing for a plural noun: people who write music

indicators.note: baroque means elaborate and convoluted, so the letters are twisted into a new pattern
without a heart means the central letters are removed
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the word with its middle two letters taken out
the five letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Poets who write ornate verse bound in uncaring covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baroque' suggests music of the Bach era, which fits the answer, but it is the anagram signal. The definition is the opening two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Composers create pieces of music by setting them down in notation, so they are people who write.

clue.text: Neglect one on purpose

blocks.note: to miss something is to fail to attend to it
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone ignores another person deliberately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On purpose' is a set phrase meaning deliberately, which hides that 'on' is a letter piece and 'purpose' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mission is a goal or vocation someone is devoted to, so it is an aim or reason for acting.

clue.text: Manage to give a speech about gym session

indicators.note: about can mean around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: to orate is to deliver a speech
PE is physical education, the school gym lesson

explanation.surface: Someone succeeds in delivering a talk on a workout class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manage to' reads as succeed in, but 'Manage' alone is the definition and 'to' is a link. PE is the school subject Physical Education.
explanation.definitionFit: To operate a business or machine is to run or control it, which is a sense of managing it.

clue.text: More old paintings rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters go the other way

blocks.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife
paintings are art

explanation.surface: A gallery turns down yet more old pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More old paintings' reads as one phrase, but 'More' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional or further, which is what more means as an adjective or adverb.

clue.text: Trim tech billionaire's status

indicators.note: trimming something cuts a bit off, here at the front

blocks.note: the word without its first letter
Elon Musk is a famous tech billionaire

explanation.surface: A reduction in the standing of a rich technology mogul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trim' could cut either end; only removing the opening T gives a usable piece. The billionaire is identified by first name only.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a level or rank in an organisation or society, so it denotes a person's standing.

clue.text: Bullish stimulant

blocks.note: first meaning: of or like a bull, from Latin taurus
second meaning: an amino acid added to energy drinks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bullish' suggests optimistic market talk, but it is meant literally: bull-like. The second meaning is a famous ingredient of Red Bull, which links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word describes bulls; as a noun it is a compound sold in energy drinks as a pick-me-up.

clue.text: Check out chief of police in hexapod

indicators.note: the chief letter of a word is its head, the first one
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: an insect has six legs, which is what hexapod means
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Examine the police chief while inside a six-legged robot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief of police' reads as a senior officer, but it means just the opening letter of 'police'.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect is to examine closely, which is what check out means as a phrasal verb.

clue.text: Compiler's back in the 12

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
the compiler, or setter, refers to herself as me

explanation.surface: The setter has returned to the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as is: the compiler is back, inside THE. Compiler for ME is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the topic of a talk or piece of writing, matching subject in its sense of topic.

clue.text: Weary sexy chap stripped — just topless

indicators.note: stripped of its outer layers, each word keeps only its inside letters
without a top means the first letter is removed

blocks.note: the inner two letters
the inner two letters
the word without its first letter

explanation.surface: A tired striptease artist ends up merely bare-chested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weary' reads as an adjective but is used as a verb, to tire out. Each piece is a word with letters stripped away.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust someone is to drain all their energy, which is a meaning of weary as a verb.

clue.text: Ship having its mast and sails overwhelmed by destiny

indicators.note: something overwhelmed is engulfed, so it ends up surrounded

blocks.note: fate is destiny
a ship's rig is its masts, sails and rigging

explanation.surface: A vessel's masts and sails are destroyed by fate in a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The rig of a sailing vessel is the arrangement of its masts and sails, so the wordplay stays within the nautical picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A frigate is a type of warship, originally a fast sailing vessel and now a naval escort.

clue.text: More luxurious, like Sir Dicky!

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for unsound or faulty, so the letters are in a broken order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something posher, like a knight called Dicky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sir Dicky' looks like a name, perhaps a knighted celebrity, but Dicky is the anagram signal: a dicky heart is a weak one.
explanation.definitionFit: Silk is a byword for luxury, so a fabric that is smoother and silkier feels richer and more opulent.

clue.text: Dine out with coppers, restricting study for freedom

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or askew, so the letters are put in a different order
restricting something holds it in, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: the four letters rearranged
copper coins are pennies; pence is the British plural
a den is a private room for reading or work, a study

explanation.surface: Eating out with police officers who keep a close eye on someone's studies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police, but here it means low-value coins: British pennies are copper-coloured.
explanation.definitionFit: Independence is the state of being self-governing and not controlled by others, which is liberty.
